title: Mobile teams, not guns, urged to defuse crises; Sewell offers advice at inquest into shooting of disturbed man: [ONT Edition]
article: Toronto police should expand a program that involves mentalhealth nurses and plainclothes officers responding to people in crisis, an approach that has proven successful downtown, a coroner's inquest has been told.

Already in place in a handful of police divisions, the mobile crisis intervention team effectively calms potentially violent situations involving mentally ill people, John Sewell, head of the Toronto Police Accountability Coalition, testified yesterday at the inquest into the June 2004 death of O'Brien Christopher\-Reid.
Created by St. Michael's Hospital and the Toronto Police Service, the team in one division responded to 703 calls, none of which involved use of force, Sewell said.

Christopher-Reid, 26, who suffered from a mental disorder, was shot four times in Edwards Gardens at Lawrence Ave. and Leslie St., after he refused to drop his knife. Three officers fired their guns as he approached them.
The province's Special Investigation Unit has cleared the officers of any criminal wrongdoing. The program did not - and still doesn't - exist in 33 Division where Christopher-Reid was shot.

Sewell, a former mayor who has written books on policing and teaches university courses on the subject, praised the program but said it only exists in a handful of divisions between 1 p.m. and 11 p.m.
"This is clearly the appropriate way to intervene," said Sewell, adding officers are often trained to be authoritative and, as a result, can intimidate people in crisis.
Sewell made five recommendations for the jury's consideration
Extend the mobile crisis intervention team approach across the city, 24 hours a day.
Set a goal to have 90 per cent of all officers aware of the program within a year so that they can call in the team when appropriate.
Train communications officers who answer 911 calls to ask more questions to help recognize when the team should be dispatched.
Provide officer training about how to handle situations with people in crisis under the auspices of the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) in conjunction with Toronto police.

Establish a committee drawn from St. Michael's, Toronto police, CAMH, the Ontario Nursing Association and psychiatric survivors to review existing training of officers as it relates to such situations.
